opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it starts with an observation about how models are trained today. Most of the signal comes from next-token prediction: you see a prefix and predict the very next token. That works remarkably well, but it pushes the model toward thinking locally, one small step at a time, and always reacting to whatever is immediately in front of it.

A lot of the problems we care about don't have that shape. Think about how a person solves a hard math problem, writes a proof, or plans a piece of code. You don't produce it left to right in one pass. You make a leap first: "I think the answer involves this invariant," or "the structure of the solution probably looks like this." Then you go back and fill in the details. The leap gives you a scaffold, and the local steps are much easier once you have it.

When a model is trained only to predict the next token, there are cases where it can latch onto shortcuts. It learns to produce text that looks locally plausible without ever building the global plan. We see this in tasks that need lookahead or planning. The model gets the early tokens wrong because the information that tells you what's right only appears later, and teacher forcing never makes it confront that. So it isn't a matter of the model needing more data or more parameters. The training objective itself isn't asking for the right kind of reasoning.

Training models to make structured leaps means giving them objectives that reward predicting further ahead, committing to intermediate goals or abstractions, and then checking themselves against those. You can do that by predicting multiple tokens or future states, by having the model generate a plan before the details, or by using objectives that aren't purely left to right. In each case you're encouraging the model to form a representation of where it's going, not just where it is.

I think this matters for a few reasons. First, it's about capability: planning and creative problem-solving seem to need it. Second, it's about robustness. Models that rely on local shortcuts tend to break in surprising ways when the distribution shifts, whereas a model that has internalized the higher-level structure of a problem tends to generalize better. And third, there's an efficiency angle. If we're going to spend a lot of compute at inference time on reasoning, it's much better if that reasoning is organized around good intermediate leaps rather than a long, meandering chain of small steps.

So, to me, it's less about making models think more and more about making them think in the right shape. That shape usually involves stepping back, making a structured guess about the big picture, and then working out the pieces.

r001.rationale: The response attributes difficulty to next-token training encouraging local reasoning and shortcuts, but does not say the leaps are left implicit in the training data.

r002.rationale: It recommends objectives that reward predicting ahead, committing to intermediate goals or abstractions, and generating a plan before details, thereby training the leap-making process.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the short version is that the way we currently train models rewards them for being good at the stuff that's already in the data, and it actively punishes them for the kind of thinking that leads to genuinely new ideas.

Let me unpack that a little. If you look at how we do pretraining, and even most of post-training, the objective is essentially: predict what comes next, where "what comes next" is drawn from the existing distribution of human text. That's fantastic for interpolation. You get a model that's extremely good at saying the plausible thing, the thing that looks like what a competent person would have written. But a lot of what we actually want from these systems, especially in science or math or any creative problem solving, is precisely the thing that would have looked *implausible* under the existing distribution. A new proof technique, a new hypothesis, a connection between two fields that nobody had bothered to make. By construction, those have low likelihood under the data, and so by construction, the training process pushes the model away from them.

So when I say "structured leaps," I'm trying to get at two things at once. The "leap" part is that we need models that are willing to go somewhere the data didn't go. But the "structured" part is really important, because a leap by itself is just noise. If you crank up the temperature on a language model, you'll get surprising outputs, but they're surprising in a useless way. What makes a human mathematician's leap valuable is that it's not random, it's constrained by a lot of structure: the leap has to be consistent with what's known, it has to be checkable, it has to actually get you somewhere. Creativity in the useful sense is novelty under constraint.

And I think the exciting thing is that we actually have levers for this now. With RL and verifiable rewards, you can in principle reward a model for arriving at a correct answer through a path that wasn't in its training data, rather than just for reproducing a path that was. You can also think about training objectives that explicitly value diversity of hypotheses, not just correctness of the single most likely one. So instead of asking "what would a typical person say here," the model learns to ask something closer to "what's a nonobvious move that I can still justify."

There's also a robustness angle to this, which is where a lot of my earlier work comes from. A model that only ever stays near the training distribution is brittle. When the world shifts, when the problem is slightly out of distribution, it has no mechanism for exploring its way to a solution. Whereas a model that's been trained to make disciplined departures from the familiar is, I think, going to be much more capable of handling situations we didn't anticipate. So I see creativity and robustness as closely linked rather than as separate goals.

The honest caveat is that we don't fully know how to do this yet. Measuring whether a leap is genuinely new versus just a recombination of memorized pieces is really hard, and if you get the incentives wrong you'll just train the model to be confidently weird. But I think the direction is clearly right. If we want these systems to contribute to knowledge rather than just summarize it, we have to stop optimizing exclusively for being typical.

r001.rationale: The response says novel ideas have low likelihood under existing data and training pushes models away from them. It does not attribute the difficulty to leaps being left implicit in the training data.

r002.rationale: The response proposes rewarding models for reaching correct answers through novel paths and learning to make nonobvious moves they can justify, communicating training for the leap-making process rather than only its outcome.

astra-6.text:
I think the motivation is that a useful reasoning step isn’t always a single token, and it isn’t always a long explanation either. Sometimes you want to work through the details, and sometimes you’ve recognized enough structure that you can jump to an intermediate conclusion and build on it.

The important part is making those jumps reliable. Can the model identify when a shortcut applies, preserve the information that matters, and check the conclusion? If we can train for that, we could get models that use their computation more effectively—spending effort on the genuinely difficult parts of a problem instead of spelling out every step indiscriminately.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that required leaps are difficult because they are left implicit in training data.

r002.rationale: It recommends training models to identify when a shortcut applies, preserve relevant information, and check the conclusion—describing how to make the leap, not just its outcome.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of reasoning involves figuring out which intermediate steps are actually useful. If you think about how we solve a problem, we don’t give every possible step equal attention. We recognize some structure, make a leap, and then check whether that leap was justified.

We’d like models to develop that ability too. A longer chain of thought doesn’t necessarily mean better reasoning; you can spend a lot of computation following an unproductive path. The hope with structured leaps is that a model can move between useful intermediate representations, while still having a way to verify those transitions. That could make reasoning both more efficient and more reliable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses useful intermediate steps and structured leaps, but does not say models struggle because those leaps are implicit in training data.

r002.rationale: The response says models should develop the ability to make structured leaps, but does not recommend training them on how to make those leaps rather than only on their outcomes.
